cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), old seed-grown Jinuo village gardens
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried maocha pressed into cakes; some households still fire the leaf in wood-heated woks, which can leave a faint smokiness.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the main harvest; autumn tea is sold as a cheaper, softer alternative.
appearance_dry: Dark, sturdy, medium-large twisted leaves with grey-white buds, pressed into a medium-tight cake.
appearance_wet: Thick, broad olive-green leaves with a few reddish stems; robust material.
taste_profile: A Yiwu-side softness crossed with Menghai-side bite: honey and flowers, a clear bitterness and some astringency that turn into sweetness within a few seconds, a medium-full body and a long warm finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Flash the first four steeps, because the astringency arrives early; after that it settles into a long, sweet session.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and village (Yanuo, Longpa, Sipu and others), mostly as small-run cakes and maocha since the six-ancient-mountains revival of the mid-2000s; before that Youle leaf went quietly into Menghai factory blends. Young (1–3 years) it is lively and slightly astringent; the 5–12-year window turns it honeyed and smooth, and old Youle sold under its own name is rare. Supply is 2005–2025, dry-stored in Jinghong or Kunming, and prices sit comfortably below Yiwu and Lao Ban Zhang.
description:
Youle is the old name for Jinuo Shan, the mountain just east of Jinghong that is home to the Jinuo people, who were recognised as China's fifty-sixth ethnic group only in 1979. It is one of the six ancient tea mountains, the one nearest the city, and its tea sits stylistically between the honeyed Yiwu side and the bitter Menghai side of Xishuangbanna.

The gardens are seed-grown old trees at around 1,100–1,400 m around Jinuo villages such as Yanuo, Longpa and Sipu, mixed with newer plantings on the lower slopes. Processing is standard sheng, and households that still fire the leaf in wood-heated woks can leave a faint smoke in the maocha that fades within a year or two. The Jinuo are also known for eating tea: a cold-dressed salad of fresh tea leaves is a traditional dish on the mountain.

In the cup Youle gives honey and flowers with a definite bitterness and an early astringency that converts fast, a medium-full body and a warm finish that stays for a while. It is more structured than Yiwu and less heavy than Bulang, and it rewards flash steeping at the start. Give it five or six years and the grip rounds into something quite Yiwu-like.

Sold by spring year and village from boutique producers, usually in small cakes, and prices are moderate because the name is less famous than its neighbours. The mountain has plenty of younger gardens, so 'Youle gushu' deserves the usual scepticism; a thick, broad leaf and a bitterness that genuinely turns sweet are the signs of the real old-tree material.

It is a useful tea for understanding the map: drink it between a Yiwu and a Bulang and you can taste where it sits.
